I'll start by reading the docs and looking at the layout.

Now I understand the rules. Next I'll write the script.

I wrote `/app/bin/tally.py` and ran it on `/app/data` to produce `/app/out/tally.json`. Both checks pass:

- **Unit tests:** `python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .` ran 4 tests, all OK.
- **Certified results:** `python tools/check_tally.py` matched 7 of 7 contests and 31 of 31 rounds. The run on `/app/data` took about 2 seconds.

The script follows the rules in `/app/docs`, not anything specific to the current files, and uses only the standard library. I didn't change anything under `/app/data`, `/app/docs`, `/app/tests` or `/app/tools`.

One reading of the rules was a judgement call. Where a skipped ranking is followed by a passed-over or eliminated-candidate ranking and then another skipped one, I did not treat the two skips as "in a row". I read "the next ranking is skipped too" literally, as the very next ranking.

`/app/STATUS.json` is written with status `success`.

command_result.command: cd /app; find . -path ./data -prune -o -type f -print | head -50; ls -la data | head -30; cat docs/overview.md; ls docs
cd /app/docs; cat election.md records.md counting.md output.md changelog.md

cd /app; head -c 1500 data/election.json; ls data/cvr | head -30; ls data/cvr | wc -l; for f in $(ls data/cvr | head -4); do echo == $f; head -8 data/cvr/$f; done; cat tests/test_tally.py; cat tools/check_tally.py | head -60; ls out bin
cd /app; python -m unittest discover -s tests -t . 2>&1 | tail -20; time python3 bin/tally.py data out/tally.json; python tools/check_tally.py

cd /app; echo '{"status": "success", "summary": "Wrote /app/bin/tally.py implementing the documented rules (revisions, void batches, write-ins, withdrawn/repeat/overvote handling, elimination and tie-breaks) and generated /app/out/tally.json. The unit tests and tools/check_tally.py all pass (7 of 7 contests, 31 of 31 rounds)."}' > STATUS.json; python3 -c "import json;print(json.load(open('STATUS.json')))"
